lesson.title: Little Albert and the Making of a Fear
lesson.summary: A conditioned emotional response is an emotional reaction, most often fear, that becomes attached to a previously neutral stimulus through classical conditioning.
lesson.body:
Not every conditioned response is as simple as a dog's salivation. Some of the most consequential conditioned responses are emotional ones: fear, anxiety, disgust, and similar reactions that get attached to formerly neutral objects, people, or places through the same acquisition process already covered. Once formed, a conditioned emotional response follows the same rules as any other conditioned response, including the potential for extinction, spontaneous recovery, and generalization to similar stimuli.

The best known, and most ethically troubling, demonstration of this comes from John Watson and Rosalie Rayner's 1920 study with an infant known as Little Albert. Before conditioning, Albert showed no fear of a white rat and would happily reach for it. Watson and Rayner then paired the rat with a loud, startling noise made by striking a steel bar, a noise that reliably frightened the child on its own, the unconditioned stimulus producing an unconditioned fear response. After several pairings of the rat with the noise, Albert began to cry and show fear at the sight of the rat alone, even with no noise at all. The rat, a previously neutral stimulus, had become a conditioned stimulus capable of triggering a conditioned emotional response.

What made the study particularly striking is that Albert's fear did not stay confined to the rat. He also showed fear reactions to other furry or white objects he had never been conditioned with directly, including a rabbit, a dog, and a fur coat, an example of the stimulus generalization already discussed, just applied to an emotional response instead of a reflex like salivation. At the level of the brain, research since then has pointed to the amygdala as a structure central to how fear gets attached to stimuli in the first place and how those emotional memories are formed and stored, though the fine details of that circuitry are still an active area of study.

It is worth being direct about the ethics here: the Little Albert study would not be approved under modern research standards. There was no systematic effort described in the original reports to remove Albert's fear afterward, and what became of him is not something the study itself resolved. It remains a foundational, and cautionary, example in the history of psychology, both for what it revealed about conditioned emotional responses and for what it revealed about the limits researchers now place on human experimentation.
